requested.title: Unauthenticated CPU-profiler start/stop endpoints disclose server paths and allow indefinite performance degradation
stopProfiler double-stop race and permanently stuck session after a failed start
Unpublished draft blog posts are served publicly because the deployed site runs with NODE_ENV=development
Blog cache invalidation can be undone by an in-flight load, pinning stale post content
Remote CHANGELOG.md is rendered into {@html} without URL-scheme sanitization, allowing javascript: links via a merged commit subject
Unbounded, never-evicted global cache keyed on caller-supplied slug (negative results cached too)
renderMarkdown output has no URL-protocol allowlist and is injected with {@html}, fed by markdown fetched from GitHub at request time

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: I traced the full registration path. `routes.ts:141` spreads the two profiler routes in only when `profilerEnabled()` is true, i.e. `process.env.MOCHI_PROFILER === '1'`. I grepped the entire repo for that variable: the only non-generated writers are `scripts/flamegraph.ts:155` (which sets it on the env of a child process it spawns itself) and `profiler.ts:5` which reads it. It appears in no Dockerfile (`Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.production`, `Dockerfile.memtest`), nowhere in `.github/workflows/build.yml`, not in `packages/docker/docker-compose.yml`, and not in any `.env`/`.env.example` — and `.dockerignore` excludes `.env*` from the image entirely. So in every deployed configuration the route keys are simply absent from the `routes` object and Bun never registers them; there is no 404-vs-403 distinction to probe, the endpoints do not exist. The only window in which they exist is a developer running `bun run flamegraph` locally, which spawns the site on port 4444 for the duration of one profiling run. Even in that window the primary impact claim fails: `/stop` returns the V8 profile via `Response.json`, but no CORS headers are set anywhere on this site (I grepped; the only CSP/cross-origin header work in the repo is `packages/support/src/embedHeaders.ts` for the newsletter iframe), so a cross-origin page can trigger the endpoint with an `` but cannot read the response — the server-path disclosure requires direct network access to the dev machine's port 4444 during a seconds-to-a-minute run. The residual 'triggering `start` degrades the process' point is real but self-inflicted and scoped to that same local run. Finally, this is the codebase's established and documented gating pattern for internal surfaces, not a deviation from it: the sibling `/_heapsnapshot` rides `HEAP_SNAPSHOTS_ENABLED`, `leak-test`/`stickers` ride `DEVELOPMENT`, and the project's own threat model records that dev surfaces are gated by flags rather than auth. The finding's own text concedes the gate; I verified it holds with no bypass, so there is no concrete attack against any deployed instance.

Both defects are unambiguous in the 26-line module. (1) Double-stop: `session` is a module-level binding, re-read at each reference rather than captured. `stopProfiler` guards on `!session` at L18, then `await`s `session.post('Profiler.stop')` at L21. Two overlapping calls both pass the L18 guard before either suspends; the first resumes, runs `Profiler.disable`, `disconnect()`, and sets `session = null` at L24. The second then resumes and evaluates `session.post('Profiler.disable')` at L22 against the now-null binding — a synchronous `TypeError` inside the async function, which the `Mochi.api` wrapper turns into a 500 — and had the ordering interleaved differently it would double-`disconnect()` the same Session. (2) Failed-start wedge: L11-L12 assign and connect before the awaits at L13-L14. If `session.connect()` throws or either `post` rejects, the rejection propagates but `session` is left non-null and un-started, so the L8 early return makes every later `startProfiler()` a silent no-op and every `stopProfiler()` either rejects from `Profiler.stop` on an unstarted profiler or returns an undefined `profile` — recoverable only by restarting the process. Neither path has a `try/catch`, an in-flight promise, or a state flag. I am keeping BUG severity rather than raising it: reachability is bounded by the same `profilerEnabled()` gate I validated for F1, and the sole caller (`scripts/flamegraph.ts:199,214`) is strictly sequential and awaits each response, so nothing in the repo triggers the race today. It is a real latent robustness defect in dev tooling, not a security issue.

I verified every link in the chain independently. `blog.ts:104` filters `p.draft` only when `includeDrafts` is falsy and `blog.ts:112` returns null for a draft only when `includeDrafts` is falsy — so the gate is entirely caller-supplied. The two public blog routes supply it conditionally: `routes.ts:229` `loadPosts({ includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT })` and `routes.ts:241` `getPost(slug, { includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT })`, with `DEVELOPMENT = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'` at `routes.ts:89`. The deployed image sets exactly that: root `Dockerfile:79` is `ENTRYPOINT [ "sh", "-c", "exec bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}" ]`, root `package.json:21` defines `dev:site` as `bun --cwd=packages/site run dev`, and `packages/site/package.json:14` defines `dev` as `NODE_ENV=development bun src/index.ts`. The Dockerfile header states the dev-mode choice is deliberate, and `.github/workflows/build.yml` confirms the site and demos legs both build `file: Dockerfile` (only the `support` leg uses `Dockerfile.production`). No env file overrides it — `.dockerignore` strips `.env*` from the build context and the root `.env` sets no `NODE_ENV` anyway. So on the live site both calls pass `includeDrafts: true`: `/blog/` lists drafts (with the `Draft` badge) and `/blog/<draft-slug>/` renders the full post to any anonymous visitor, and `og/resolve.ts:34` mints a social card for it. The code's own comments assert the opposite invariant (`feed.ts:31`, `docs.ts:299`, `docs.ts:327-329`, `blogComponents.prerender.ts:5`), and the existing tests (`blog.test.ts`, `feed.test.ts`, `sitemap.test.ts`) only cover the library default — nothing asserts the route behaviour, which is why the drift survived. I confirmed the finding's own caveat: none of the four files in `packages/site/src/blog/` carries `draft: true`, so nothing is leaking at this instant. I am still calling this a true positive and holding MEDIUM: the access-control decision is genuinely inverted in the shipped configuration, the exposure is one commit of embargoed content away, and the `draft` flag plus `Draft` badge exist precisely to stage such content — an authorisation control that is off in production is a real defect regardless of how many records currently sit behind it.

The shape is exactly as described and there is no guard anywhere in the module. `loadAllPosts()` returns early on a populated `cache.posts` (L51), then suspends repeatedly — `glob.scan` (L57), `Bun.file().text()` (L64), and `parsePostFrontmatter`'s `mdsvexCompile` (L65) per file — before writing `cache.posts` and `cache.bySlug` at L97-98. `clearBlogCaches()` (L35-38) nulls both synchronously and is subscribed to `file:change` at `index.ts:37-44`. Because JS interleaves only at await points, the invalidation can land between L64's read of a file's pre-edit bytes and L97's assignment; the assignment then reinstates the pre-edit snapshot over a cache that was just invalidated, and nothing re-clears it. The blast radius is slightly wider than one post: `index.ts:40-42` also calls `clearFeedCache()` and `clearDocsCaches()`, and `feed.ts`/`buildSitemapXml` repopulate from this same `cache.posts`, so the stale body propagates into the feed and sitemap caches too, persisting until an unrelated later edit happens to re-trigger the watcher outside the window. There is no in-flight dedupe either, so concurrent cold loads also redo the whole filesystem scan. I agree with BUG severity and with the finding's low-impact framing: the `file:change` subscription is inside `index.ts:28`'s `NODE_ENV === 'development'` block, and although the deployed container also runs with `NODE_ENV=development`, nothing rewrites `src/blog/*.md` at runtime there, so in practice this is a dev-server hot-reload staleness bug with a window of one `loadAllPosts()` pass (four small files) and it self-heals on the next save. Real defect, correctly classified as a correctness nit rather than a security issue.

I verified the sink and every mitigation claim against library source rather than taking the finding's word for it. `changelog.ts:18` fetches `CHANGELOG_URL` (raw.githubusercontent.com, `refs/heads/main`) at request time, L46 pipes it through `renderMarkdown`, and `Docs.svelte:63` injects the result with `{@html html}` for `/docs/changelog/`. No sanitizer exists in the project: `rehype-sanitize`, `sanitize-html` and `DOMPurify` are absent from every `package.json`, and the only `*sanitize*` module in `node_modules` is the transitive `micromark-util-sanitize-uri`. Raw-tag injection is in fact blocked, and incidentally so: `mdsvex/dist/main-Bo3idoP1.js:24556-24559` configures `remark2rehype` with `allowDangerousHtml: true` (so HTML becomes hast `raw` nodes), but `markdown.ts:56` calls `toHtml(tree)` with no options and `hast-util-to-html/lib/index.js:204` defaults `allowDangerousHtml` to `false`, whose `handle/raw.js` then routes raw nodes through the `text` serializer. URL schemes, however, are never checked: `mdast-util-to-hast/lib/handlers/link.js` sets `href` via `normalizeUri` only (percent-encoding, not the protocol-filtering `sanitizeUri`), mdsvex's own `external` plugin is configured `{target: false, rel: ['nofollow']}` and only adds `rel`, and this project's `rehypeExternalLinks.ts:17-19` classifies any non-http(s) protocol as 'internal' and returns before touching the node. So `[x](javascript:alert(1))` in the changelog serialises as a live `<a href="javascript:alert(1)">` on https://mochi.fast/docs/changelog/, and I confirmed there is no CSP on `packages/site` to stop it (the repo's only `Content-Security-Policy` is `packages/support/src/embedHeaders.ts`'s `frame-ancestors`). The untrusted-input path is genuine: the live `packages/mochi/CHANGELOG.md` shows release-please writing commit subjects verbatim into markdown bullets, with only Handlebars' HTML escaping applied (visible as `svelte-shaker >=0.18.1`) — which touches `< > & " ' \``  but not `[`, `]`, `(`, `)` or `:`, so markdown link syntax in a squash-merged PR title survives intact. Preconditions keep real-world likelihood low (a maintainer must merge a PR whose title embeds the link, and a visitor must click it) and the site carries no session worth stealing beyond the `hunter2` demo cookie, which is why I am not raising severity — but the defect is real, the sink is unguarded, and the impact is script execution in the mochi.fast origin.

Every element of the chain checks out. `cache.demoLlmsTxt` is a plain `Map` inside the `pinGlobal('__mochi_site_docs_cache__')` object (`docs.ts:55-66`), so it is process-wide and survives duplicate bundled copies. `getDemoLlmsTxt` (L201-210) memoizes unconditionally, including misses — `buildDemoLlmsTxt` returns `null` at L214 for an unknown slug and L208 still inserts it, as the comment states. The only eviction is `clearDocsCaches()`'s `.clear()` at L75, reachable solely from the dev-only `file:change` subscription at `index.ts:30-34`, which filters on `.md` files under `DOCS_DIR` — nothing rewrites those at runtime in the container, so in a deployed process the map is append-only forever. The key is attacker-controlled: of the three call sites, `demoLlmsRoutes` and `buildDemosTxt` both iterate fixed slugs from `internalDemos()`, but `mcp.ts:57` forwards the request's `slug` straight through for `type === 'demo'`, and its schema at `mcp.ts:51` is `v.string()` inside an unbounded `v.array()` — no length, charset, or array-size limit. `/mcp` and `/mcp/` are registered unconditionally at `routes.ts:347-348` with no `rateLimit` option, and I confirmed in `Mochi.ts:801-829` that `buildLimiter` returns `null` when neither the route nor `Mochi.serve({ rateLimit })` supplies a config — `packages/site/src/index.ts` sets neither, so the endpoint is entirely unmetered. I also read `@tmcp/transport-http/src/index.js`: `#handle_post` checks only `Content-Type: application/json` before `request.clone().json()`, imposes no body cap, and `tmcp` has no initialize-before-call requirement (no 'not initialized' guard exists) and no OAuth is configured, so a single anonymous POST reaches `get_section`. Concrete attack: POST a `tools/call` for `get_section` with a large `sections` array of `{"type":"demo","slug":"<unique>"}` entries; every distinct slug is retained permanently as a UTF-16 Map key with per-entry overhead exceeding the ~31 bytes it cost to send, so the retained heap grows faster than the request body and repeats are free. Even if an upstream nginx `client_max_body_size` caps bodies at 1 MB, ~32k permanent entries per request with no quota reaches a container OOM in a few hundred requests; the unbounded `Promise.all` fan-out over the same array adds a transient CPU/allocation spike. MEDIUM is the right severity for an unauthenticated resource-exhaustion DoS. One note on framing: the `cache-key-poisoning` slug is a misnomer — distinct slugs cannot displace legitimate entries — but the substantive impact the description argues (unbounded, never-evicted growth driven by unvalidated input) is confirmed.

This is the same underlying weakness as F5 viewed from the renderer rather than the caller; because the rules scope duplicates to a single file and this one is anchored in `markdown.ts` while F5 is anchored in `changelog.ts`, I am giving it its own verdict, and the analysis confirms it. `renderMarkdown` (L51-66) captures the hast tree inside a rehype plugin and serialises it with a bare `toHtml(tree)` at L56, returning a string its only consumer treats as trusted HTML. I confirmed the two halves of the claim in library source: `hast-util-to-html/lib/index.js:204` defaults `allowDangerousHtml` to `false` and `lib/handle/raw.js` falls through to the `text` serializer, so the `raw` nodes mdsvex produces (it sets `allowDangerousHtml: true` on its own `remark2rehype` at `mdsvex/dist/main-Bo3idoP1.js:24558`) are escaped — meaning the bare `toHtml` call is load-bearing and undocumented, exactly as the finding says; but no stage filters URL schemes, because `mdast-util-to-hast/lib/handlers/link.js` applies only `normalizeUri` and `rehypeExternalLinks.ts:17-19` returns early on any non-http(s) protocol, treating it as 'internal'. There is no CSP on `packages/site` (the repo's only `Content-Security-Policy` is `packages/support/src/embedHeaders.ts`) and no sanitizer dependency anywhere in the tree. I verified by grep that `renderMarkdown` has exactly one caller — `changelog.ts:46`, on text fetched from `raw.githubusercontent.com` at request time — and that `Docs.svelte:63` injects it with `{@html html}` behind an eslint-disable asserting 'first-party markdown', an assumption that is true of the file's provenance but not of its contents: the live `packages/mochi/CHANGELOG.md` shows release-please emitting commit subjects verbatim with only Handlebars HTML escaping, which leaves `[`, `]`, `(`, `)` and `:` untouched, so a squash-merged PR title can carry a markdown link. The practical exploit therefore needs a merged PR title plus a victim click, which keeps likelihood low, but the gap in this file is real and is the correct place to fix it: a function whose own docstring scopes it to 'markdown that arrives at runtime' should not assume a trusted author, and any second caller would inherit the same unguarded sink.
